mathgap.title: Signed difference equality
mathgap.principle: When a statement equates one signed difference to another, translate it directly as (A - B) = (C - D) preserving the order of names. This treats the difference as signed, allowing negative values.
mathgap.when_to_apply: Whenever you encounter a sentence of the form "the number of X that A has more than B is equal to the difference between the number of Y that C and D have".
mathgap.example: Treating "Pat has more than Leone" as an absolute difference |Pat‑Leone| instead of the signed difference (Pat‑Leone).

mathgap.title: Direct count assignment at point of mention
mathgap.principle: When a statement directly gives a count for a person, set that person's current count to the stated number at that point in the sequence, before any later transfers modify it.
mathgap.when_to_apply: When you read a clause like "Lorenzo has 15 pineapples".
mathgap.example: Ignoring the explicit count and leaving Lorenzo's variable undefined.

mathgap.title: Non‑negative integer check
mathgap.principle: All item counts must be non‑negative integers; after solving, discard any solution that yields a negative or fractional count for any person.
mathgap.when_to_apply: After you have derived values for all variables, before reporting the final answer.
mathgap.example: Accepting a solution where Eddie ends up with –3 pineapples.

mathgap.title: Conditional transfer handling
mathgap.principle: For a transfer that is conditioned on a prior state, first evaluate the condition using the current counts; only if the condition holds should the transfer be applied.
mathgap.when_to_apply: When a statement reads like "If X has more than Y, then X gives N to Z".
mathgap.example: Applying the transfer regardless of whether the condition "X has more than Y" is true.

mathgap.title: Directionality of more/fewer statements
mathgap.principle: Interpret "X has N more than Y" as X ‑ Y = N (i.e., X = Y + N) and "X has N fewer than Y" as X ‑ Y = ‑N.
mathgap.when_to_apply: Whenever a sentence contains the phrase "has N more/fewer than".
mathgap.example: Reading "X has 5 more than Y" as X = Y ‑ 5.

mathgap.title: Split‑all handling
mathgap.principle: When a statement says "X splits all the items she owns equally among Y and Z", give each of Y and Z half of X's current count and set X's count to zero.
mathgap.when_to_apply: When you encounter a clause of the form "X splits all the items she owns equally among Y and Z".
mathgap.example: Leaving X with its original count after the split instead of setting X to zero.

mathgap.title: Targeted constraint extraction for queried variable
mathgap.principle: When the goal is to find a specific person's count, first gather all equations that directly involve that person (or relate them through known differences) and solve using only those, avoiding unnecessary work on unrelated variables.
mathgap.when_to_apply: At the start of solving, after reading the question, identify the target person and collect relevant constraints.
mathgap.example: Solving the entire system of equations even though only a few involve Arleen.

mathgap.title: Sequential transfer handling with updated counts
mathgap.principle: When a transfer statement appears, immediately subtract the transferred amount from the giver and add it to the receiver, so that any subsequent statements use the updated counts.
mathgap.when_to_apply: Whenever you read a clause like "Eddie gives 33 pineapples to Waymon".
mathgap.example: Applying a later transfer before an earlier one, causing Waymon's count to be wrong for earlier equations.

mathgap.title: Substitution of known signed differences into signed difference equalities
mathgap.principle: If a signed difference on one side of an equality is already known from a direct statement, substitute that numeric value into the equation to simplify and solve for unknowns.
mathgap.when_to_apply: When you have an equation like (Kari ‑ Sammie) = (Arleen ‑ Chelsey) and you already know Kari ‑ Sammie = 10.
mathgap.example: Leaving the equation (Kari ‑ Sammie) = (Arleen ‑ Chelsey) unsimplified despite knowing the left‑hand side equals 10.

mathgap.title: Chronological evaluation of statements
mathgap.principle: Process the list of statements in order, using the current counts at each step. Earlier equations must be evaluated with counts before any later transfers, and later equations must use counts after earlier transfers have been applied.
mathgap.when_to_apply: While iterating through the problem text, before translating each sentence into an equation, ensure all prior transfers have been applied and no future transfers have been applied yet.
mathgap.example: Using Waymon's post‑transfer count of 41 in the equation that appears before the "Eddie gives 33 pineapples to Waymon" statement.

mathgap.description: Treating signed difference statements as absolute differences
mathgap.why_it_happens: The model assumes "has more than" always yields a positive difference, ignoring that the signed difference can be negative when the order contradicts earlier facts.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Always translate "X has N more than Y" as the signed equation X ‑ Y = N, even if X is later known to be smaller; keep the sign as written.

mathgap.description: Ignoring the sequential order of transfers
mathgap.why_it_happens: The model treats all statements as describing the final state, so it applies transfers out of order or uses post‑transfer counts for earlier equations.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Maintain a running state of counts; apply each transfer immediately when it appears and evaluate subsequent statements with the updated state.

mathgap.description: Assuming explicit counts are final after all transfers
mathgap.why_it_happens: Direct count statements are taken as immutable, so later transfers that affect those persons are ignored.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Treat direct counts as the current value at that point; allow later transfer statements to modify those values.

mathgap.description: Misinterpreting 'increase by N times' as addition rather than multiplication
mathgap.why_it_happens: The phrasing is read as a linear increase, leading to adding N instead of multiplying.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Recognize the phrase "increase by N times" as a multiplicative factor: new = old × N.

mathgap.description: Misinterpreting split‑all statements as leaving the original person with zero even when they are a recipient
mathgap.why_it_happens: The model applies the split to the recipients but forgets to also set the splitter's count to zero.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: When "X splits all the items she owns equally among Y and Z" occurs, set X's count to zero after giving each half to Y and Z.
